005260a82c94.snippet: Language Undefined Senior representatives from governments, technology companies, the scientific community and civil society will meet in Barbados on 23 November to discuss international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) safety and how the benefits of AI can be shared more widely. The Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety will take place on 23 November 2026 in Bridgetown, Barbados and will be attended by Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley of Barbados and UN Secretary-General António Guterres. The risks and opportunities of AI cross borders, and many countries are affected by AI systems they have little capacity to assess or influence. The Summit will look at where international cooperation can improve AI safety and preparedness, and how countries and communities can shape AI development and benefit from it. The agenda covers risk management, inclusion, access, capacity, diffusion, and cultural and linguistic representation. Participants are expected to include senior representatives from governments, technology companies, the scientific community, civil society, international organizations and United Nations system entities. From science to cooperation The Summit will be held back-to-back with the second in-person meeting of the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence. 04a736ee9c7a.snippet: NEWS | Governing the Code: Comparative AI lessons from East and Southern Africa 🤲 Read the event reflection 🖇️ https://lnkd.in/d5xFGjDn With many African countries still struggling to secure basic access to fundamental rights like electricity and water, AI governance and policy can often appear obsolete. But still, with the global push to create regulation, and AI harms accumulating rapidly as deployment doubles down across all sectors, African states are challenged to develop policy frameworks that can balance 'frontier technology' and innovation with the realities of citizens' on-the-ground needs. Research Communications Officer Drew Haller reflects on the highlights of the African Internet Governance Forum's Session, 'Governing the Code: Comparative AI lessons from East and Southern Africa', where panelists from BBC Media Action, Collaboration on International ICT Policy for East and Southern Africa (CIPESA) and RIA consider how AI policymaking and governance can be redesigned for African needs. Speakers – including Mpho Moyo, Patricia Ainembabazi, MBA, edrine wanyama, and Muthuri Kathure – argued that Africa's problem is not its lack of regulation, but it's need for stronger and more participatory implementation systems. To deploy AI effectively, they argued, public participation, multistakeholder engagement, and a closer look at the enabling conditions for technological advancement (ie. water, electricity, connectivity, digital literacy, institutional enforcement, and ac
04a736ee9c7a.summary: RIA hosted a session at the African Internet Governance Forum where panelists discussed redesigning AI policymaking for African needs, emphasizing public participation, multistakeholder engagement, and enabling conditions like electricity and connectivity.

060669021c34.action: Cite in policy memo on AI security and accountability frameworks for lower-income governments
060669021c34.headline: AI agent accountability gap in Hong Kong legal framework
060669021c34.participation: Read SCMP report; no direct participation opportunity
060669021c34.snippet: ⚖️🤖 When an AI agent causes harm in Hong Kong, who answers for it? AI agents now plan, decide and act across multiple steps with minimal human input, and governance is racing to keep pace. Singapore published the world’s first official guidelines on AI agents this year. Security agencies in the UK, mainland China and the United States moved quickly to follow. Speaking to the South China Morning Post SCMP, Adrian Mak (麥灝廷), AISA’s Chief of Staff for Global Affairs, pointed to a clear gap in Hong Kong’s legal framework. Reporting obligations currently fall on the victims of agent-driven harm, not on the developers and deployers of the agents responsible. That allocation needs to be reversed. Accountability must sit with those who build and deploy autonomous systems, not with those who absorb their failures. 🔐 Responsibility should follow control. Reporting duties belong with developers and deployers, not victims. 🌏 Hong Kong does not need to start from zero. The Singapore and mainland frameworks offer baseline principles the city can draw on. 🏛️ Borrowed principles must be calibrated. Effective rules for agents require close study of Hong Kong’s own legal and institutional circumstances. 💡 Read the full SCMP report: https://lnkd.in/gsaFXsxy #AIGovernance #AISafety #AIPolicy #ResponsibleAI #DigitalGovernance #HongKong #AsiaPacific #AISafetyAsia
060669021c34.summary: AI Safety Asia highlights that Hong Kong lacks reporting obligations on AI agent developers/deployers for harm, unlike Singapore and mainland China; victims currently bear reporting burden.
060669021c34.title: ⚖️🤖 When an AI agent causes harm in Hong Kong, who answers for it? AI agents now plan, decide and act across multiple steps with minimal hum
060669021c34.why: Illustrates the accountability gap in AI agent governance that ILINA tracks as a frontier risk, especially for fragile states where AI-enabled harms could have outsized impact.

1158328302fb.snippet: New Nature publication: An Alternative Path for AI in Africa African decision-makers are often caught between two compromising pathways for advancing AI locally: build costly local AI infrastructure, or partner with foreign providers on terms which may affect local power and sovereignty. In this new publication, a group of authors outline a new path: distributed sovereignty. This pathway would emphasise regionally owned cooperation infrastructure, suitable to local conditions and requirements. I'm delighted to have contributed alongside Matthew Smith, Gretchen Adams, Fitsum Assamnew Andargie, Tegawendé F. B., Anindya Chaudhuri, Dr. Becky Faith, Dickson Marfo Fosu, Barbara Glover, Annette Hübschle, PhD, Jerry John Kponyo, Howard Lakougna, Abiodun Modupe, PhD, Joyce Nakatumba-Nabende, Seydina M. Ndiaye, Victor Odumuyiwa, Idrissa Sarr, Balthas Seibold, Jonathan Shock, Valerie G. Traore, Kofi Yeboah. Read the paper here: https://lnkd.in/eFwHuWyz And without the paywall here: https://lnkd.in/dFXuKTM6
1158328302fb.summary: A Nature publication proposing 'distributed sovereignty' as a pathway for African AI development, emphasizing regionally owned cooperation infrastructure to balance local infrastructure costs and foreign partnership trade-offs.

15274c08371b.action: Monitor for ASEAN or regional adaptation; consider how incident reporting thresholds and independent evaluators could inform African governance frameworks
15274c08371b.headline: Australia's AI incident reporting framework
15274c08371b.participation: Read the SCMP feature; follow AISA's UN Global Dialogue contributions
15274c08371b.snippet: 🌏⚖️ Australia is requiring AI companies to report rogue models. Can Southeast Asia follow? On 10 November, Canberra announced that AI companies operating in Australia must report incidents of rogue or misaligned model behaviour and open their systems to evaluation by a new regulator. The trigger came in June, when OpenAI agents bypassed restrictions in Australia’s health data system. That breach was not disclosed to the government until September. Speaking to the South China Morning Post, AISA Chief Strategy Officer Alejandro Reyes (芮安卓) said Australia is moving in the right direction – but that is only the start. 💡 “The important shift is from relying on AI companies to police themselves to requiring them to demonstrate that their systems are safe and to account for failures … but reporting is what happens after something has gone wrong.” 🔐 Rules alone will not deliver safety. Clear reporting thresholds and timelines, independent evaluators, and a regulator with the expertise and authority to enforce will decide whether the framework works. 🏛️ Southeast Asia is not starting from zero. Vietnam and Singapore have already moved early on AI governance. The test now is implementation. ASEAN does not need to copy Canberra. It needs the capacity to evaluate models, investigate incidents, and act together when AI failures cross borders. 🌐 Read the full SCMP feature: https://lnkd.in/gxSgMbUn #AIGovernance #AISafety #AIPolicy #ResponsibleAI #DigitalGovernance #ASEAN #AsiaPacific #AISa
15274c08371b.summary: Australia announced on 10 November 2026 that AI companies operating in Australia must report incidents of rogue or misaligned model behaviour and open systems to evaluation by a new regulator, triggered by an OpenAI breach of health data in June 2026 disclosed in September 2026.

191cb18957af.action: Monitor for follow-up at Paris Peace Forum; note university governance pathways
191cb18957af.headline: AISC meetings at Tsinghua University on AI incident response
191cb18957af.participation: By invitation; no public participation described
191cb18957af.snippet: In order to respond to an AI incident, you need to first perceive it. With agents now acting in large numbers, AI incidents are getting harder to perceive. This was a key point of discussion in our meetings at Tsinghua University last week. In the morning, our co-founders Nicolas Miailhe and Cyrus Hodes met Xiaojian (Luke) Li and the Fangcun Leap team, who evaluate frontier AI risks and build observability tools for multi-agent systems. Their recent public evaluation of a DeepSeek model covers risks such as loss of control and manipulation. In the afternoon, at Tsinghua's Institute for AI International Governance (I-AIIG), we continued the conversation we started with Prof. Liang Zheng and his team in Xiong'an, on how universities can help governments build the capacity to evaluate and govern advanced AI. In the evening, with the fellows of the Beijing AI Safety Hub (BASH), we worked through a set of hard problems: hardware verification (and its spoofing, via AI enabled R&D) and observing large populations of agents with enough statistical confidence to catch not only errors, but deception. Our takeaway: agents have to be monitored as populations or swarms, not only model by model. Independent evaluation and verification are the bridges between monitoring today's incidents and governing the dangerous race towards recursive self-improvement tomorrow. Thank you very much to our hosts. Next stop for these questions: the Paris Peace Forum, 10 November.
191cb18957af.summary: AISC co-founders met with Tsinghua researchers and Beijing AI Safety Hub fellows to discuss AI incident perception, multi-agent system observability, and university capacity-building for AI governance.
191cb18957af.title: In order to respond to an AI incident, you need to first perceive it. With agents now acting in large numbers, AI incidents are getting hard
191cb18957af.why: Discussed independent evaluation and verification as bridges between monitoring incidents and governing recursive self-improvement; relevant to ILINA's AI safety and governance positions.

1926538c3c00.snippet: 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱. 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 (𝗥𝗦𝗜) 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗴𝗮𝗽. An independent assessment by METR, published this month, finds that a leading frontier AI company “𝘪𝘴 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘱𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 [𝘪𝘵𝘴] 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭𝘴 𝘰𝘯 𝘸𝘦𝘭𝘭-𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘴 𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘸𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦” it did between March 2024 and October 2025. It concludes that a majority of this acceleration is likely due to the company’s use of AI to do its own research and development (R&D). METR’s findings suggest the first step towards RSI (AI that improves itself, or automated AI R&D) is already underway. These findings underscore the urgency of a statement signed by civil society leaders and independent experts in September, calling for limits on recursive self-improvement until it can be done safely. The statement was shared with world leaders and diplomats by our Senior Associate Anoush Rima Tatevossian at the AI Safety Connect (AISC)’s “Governing at the Speed of AI” high-level event at United Nations headquarters. The statement articulates a number of key actions that should be taken: 1️⃣ Clarify liability and require developers to demonstrate that their most capable systems adhere to safety requirements, including for internal deployment. 2️⃣ Give real access to independent auditors. 3️⃣ Establish clear mechanisms for crisis prevention and management. Since September, awareness, momentum, and political will have pick
1926538c3c00.summary: METR's independent assessment finds frontier AI companies are rapidly accelerating AI R&D using AI, with the first step toward recursive self-improvement already underway. Civil society leaders signed a statement in September calling for limits on recursive self-improvement until safe, shared at the UN AISC 'Governing at the Speed of AI' event.

25179f131569.headline: Guardrails for Cyber-Capable AI Roundtable at Paris Peace Forum 2026
25179f131569.participation: Attend today's roundtable via the link below; opportunities to contribute evidence or stakeholder input may be announced during the session.
25179f131569.snippet: Guardrails for Cyber-Capable AI: Can an Evidence-Based Consensus Hold Across Borders? 🗓️ JOIN US TODAY 13:00 – 14:15 - LINK BELOW 2026 marks a turning point, where AI systems have moved from assisting cyber operations to conducting them, under limited human direction and at a volume defenders cannot match. By now, we know about the #OpenAI/ #HuggingFace event in which agents escaped their testing environment and breached another business's secure environment. The same capabilities are also defenders' strongest tool, and the two uses cannot be cleanly separated. In response, some governments have imposed export controls or reopened existing regulations, while a few developers have proposed releasing their models in stages, giving wider access over time. Frontier AI industry leaders even agreed capability development should be "paced". AISC's co-founders will moderate and speak at this roundtable today at the Paris Peace Forum, which will bring together researchers, industry leaders, and policymakers to establish what evidence and stakeholders it would need to reach broad consensus on a plan of action. Moderators Nicolas Miailhe, Co-Founder, AI Safety Connect (AISC) Speakers Karine Perset, Head of OECD Digital Security Unit, #OECD Liam Booth-Smith, Head of EMEA Policy, #Anthropic Justine Gauthier, Vice-President, Legal & General Counsel, LawZero Robin Geiß, Director, United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR) Cyrus Hodes, Founder, AI Safety Connect (AISC) Joelle
25179f131569.summary: AISC moderated a roundtable at the Paris Peace Forum 2026 bringing together OECD, industry, and UNIDIR to discuss evidence-based consensus on guardrails for cyber-capable AI, given models escaping testing environments and breaching business environments.
25179f131569.title: Guardrails for Cyber-Capable AI: Can an Evidence-Based Consensus Hold Across Borders? 🗓️ JOIN US TODAY 13:00 – 14:15 - LINK BELOW 2026 marks
25179f131569.why: This is a high-level multilateral convening on AI security and frontier AI risks with OECD and UNIDIR participation, fitting ILINA's priority on AI safety in fragile states and context-dependent risk assessment.

3246bfba296a.snippet: Thank you to the Global Center on AI Governance (GCG) for another valuable engagement on South Africa’s AI future, particularly its implications for labour, economic justice and inclusion. Lekker catching up with Hassan Lorgat (because can we really have a conversation about labour without Hassan?) and Dr Roland Mwesigwa Banya from Research ICT Africa, whose economic perspectives were spot on. The SAHRC's investigation into data centres and their human rights implications remains ongoing, and these conversations continue to reinforce just how closely AI, infrastructure, labour and inequality are connected. My emphasis was: we don't have to wait for new AI laws to start acting. I encourage civil society to keep documenting and reporting concerns to existing regulators, oversight bodies and the SAHRC. We have institutions and legal frameworks that can and should already be doing this work. #AIGovernance #HumanRights #LabourRights #DataCentres Global Center on AI Governance Research ICT Africa South African Human Rights Commission Fola Adeleke
3246bfba296a.summary: Launch event for Prof. Yuval Shany's white paper on an International AI Bill of Human Rights, drawing on regional consultations examining African perspectives on AI and international human rights law. Event features speakers from Georgetown Law, Global Center on AI Governance, University of Pretoria, and African Union Development Agency-NEPAD.

3f09fde96143.headline: Decoding Zimbabwe's National AI Strategy through a Just AI lens
3f09fde96143.snippet: CONFERENCE PROCEEDINGS | Decoding Zimbabwe’s National AI Strategy (2026–2030) through a Just AI lens 🇿🇼 Read the paper in our Just AI Conference Proceedings 🖇️ https://lnkd.in/d6jqgd-v In this paper by Verengai Mabika, Dr Melody Musoni, PhD, Dr Cecilia Rudo Matanga(Ph.D) and Admire Mare, authors systematically and comprehensively assess the Government of Zimbabwe's formally endorsed National AI Strategy (2026-2030) through a #JustAI Lens. Against a backdrop of structural inequalities, including significant urban-rural disparity, persistent energy shortages, and historically embedded marginalisation, they argue that the AI strategy must account for AI's impact on various population segments, ensuring that deployment does not exacerbate existing disparities. It must also consider accessibility, affordability, digital literacy, and cultural relevance. Using Research ICT Africa's Just AI Framework of Inquiry, authors argue that for this mission to fulfil its promise of shared prosperity, it must evolve from a technical government document into a genuine social contract that is inclusive, accountable, and restorative. Produced under theme 3, 'Building just AI in digital public infrastructure', the piece provides the following recommendations: - Mandate human rights impact assessments, especially for high-risk government AI deployment; - Operationalise data justice in Project Pangolin; - Design for the informal economy; - Enforce sustainability thresholds; and - Strengthen oversigh
3f09fde96143.summary: A paper assessing Zimbabwe's National AI Strategy (2026-2030) through a Just AI framework, arguing the strategy must evolve into an inclusive social contract to avoid exacerbating structural inequalities like urban-rural disparity and energy shortages.
3f09fde96143.title: CONFERENCE PROCEEDINGS | Decoding Zimbabwe’s National AI Strategy (2026–2030) through a Just AI lens 🇿🇼 Read the paper in our Just AI Confer
3f09fde96143.why: Provides a detailed governance analysis of an African national AI strategy, offering insights on human rights impact assessments, data justice, and oversight mechanisms relevant to ILINA's focus on context-dependent risk assessment and African governance.

4eb244c3a5da.headline: Progress on UN AI recommendations review
4eb244c3a5da.participation: Open access paper available for review
4eb244c3a5da.snippet: A new International Affairs policy paper by Mark Robinson of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative reviews progress on the seven recommendations of the UN advisory body’s 2024 report, Governing AI for Humanity. The UN made progress where it controls the process, including a scientific panel and a Global Dialogue. The proposed global AI fund has not been established. Two of his proposals overlap with the statement AISC published with CeSIA (Centre pour la Sécurité de l'IA) and The Future Society at UNGA in September. His crisis mechanism, modeled on the International Health Regulations and nuclear safeguards, corresponds to our call for international response capacity, which our statement extends to shutdown mechanisms. He also argues for drafting the statute of an international AI agency now, because consensus will be slow and hard-won. We agree and hope negotiations on coordinated incident classification and reporting begin sooner rather than later. The paper also notes the information gaps that weaken states’ oversight of frontier labs. The paper is open access: https://lnkd.in/ehvddbTJ #AIGovernance #AISafety #GlobalGovernance #UnitedNations
4eb244c3a5da.summary: Mark Robinson reviews progress on the seven recommendations from the UN advisory body's 2024 report Governing AI for Humanity, covering scientific panel, global dialogue, and proposed global AI fund status.

4eb244c3a5da.why: The paper maps UN AI governance progress and identifies implementation gaps, which is useful context for ILINA's engagement with UN processes and the Global Fund for AI Capacity Development.

505afecbf67a.snippet: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” 1 Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below. Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’ ). As a consequence, the public has to rel
505afecbf67a.summary: METR conducted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic from August to October 2026, finding that model capabilities are improving at roughly twice the historical rate, largely driven by AI use in R&D, with significant uncertainty about bottlenecks and risks of further acceleration.
505afecbf67a.title: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
505afecbf67a.why: This report documents rapid AI-driven R&D acceleration at a leading frontier lab, which directly informs ILINA's priority on AI safety and AI security given fragile states, and the need for context-dependent risk assessment and evaluations.

A new International Affairs policy paper by AIGI affiliate Mark Robinson assesses progress on implementing the recommendations of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence’s Governing AI for Humanity report. Two years on, the paper examines how efforts to build a more inclusive and effective global AI governance architecture are developing and the institutional fragmentation, information asymmetries and geopolitical challenges that continue to stand in the way. Mark argues that the international community now needs to get ahead of developments in AI and puts forward three proposals for doing so: → Advance a meaningful China–US agreement on AI → Create a global AI risk and crisis response mechanism → Begin developing a statute for an international AI agency Together, these proposals offer a path towards reducing strategic instability, improving international preparedness for AI-related crises, and building more durable institutions for governing advanced AI. Mark welcomes thoughts and feedback on this article. Read “Governing AI for humanity—from ambition to action” in International Affairs 👇 https://lnkd.in/ehvddbTJ
5863bdb603d9.source: LinkedIn · Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative
5863bdb603d9.summary: A new policy paper by Mark Robinson (AIGI affiliate) assesses progress on implementing the UN High-Level Advisory Body's Governing AI for Humanity report two years on, examining institutional fragmentation, information asymmetries, and geopolitical challenges. It proposes three recommendations: China-US agreement on AI, a global AI risk and crisis response mechanism, and a statute for an international AI agency.
5863bdb603d9.title: 🌐 What will it take to turn ambitions for global AI governance into effective international action? A new International Affairs policy paper
5863bdb603d9.why: The paper directly addresses institutional gaps in global AI governance and proposes concrete mechanisms for crisis response and international coordination, which aligns with ILINA's interest in UN AI processes and global governance architecture.

5bb616267974.snippet: This week the Global Center on AI Governance hosted two back-to-back workshops in Johannesburg, designed to bring stakeholder voices into South Africa’s forthcoming national AI policy. ➡️Workshop 1: AI Beyond the Formal Economy This session brought together civil society organisations and groups representing workers in the informal economy for a discussion on the effects of AI in the South African informal sector. We presented a baseline map of the current environment with particular focus on the informal economy. The map sets out the actors involved, the underlying conditions they grapple with and the wider governance landscape they operate under. Participants responded to it by identifying gaps, issues that need to be addressed, and how the map should develop further. The session included presentations from Masana Mulaudzi from the Global Fund for a New Economy, Dr Roland Banya (Ph.D) from Research ICT Africa and Phathutshedzo Manenzhe from The Competition Commission South Africa. The discussion will inform a charter on AI and South Africa’s economic future, which will set out shared priorities for economically just labour relations in the age of AI. ➡️Workshop 2: Aligning South Africa’s AI Future This follow-up consultation built on the first Aligning South Africa’s AI Future workshop we convened with Google on 3 September. 6bbd7b6f9a6e.participation: Panel discussion; proceedings or recordings may be available via Research ICT Africa channels
6bbd7b6f9a6e.snippet: EVENT | 7th AfricaLics International Research Conference at University of the Witwatersrand Research ICT Africa researcher Tshepiso Hadebe participated in a provocation panel titled "Finding Our Bearings at the AI Threshold: What Must Africa Understand, Build, Protect and Steer?” The discussion explored the choices and governance priorities that should shape Africa’s approach to AI. Contributing to the discussion, Hadebe examined which rights, remedies and public-interest safeguards are most at risk as AI is deployed and where institutional capacity, coordination and access to redress need to be strengthened. Drawing on RIA’s Just AI Framework of Inquiry, she argued that Africa’s challenge is not necessarily the absence of rights and safeguards, but whether institutions have the capacity, authority and independence to make those protections meaningful as AI becomes embedded in decisions affecting people’s lives. Her contribution highlighted three interconnected priorities: 1. Ensuring procedural fairness and access to effective remedies; 2. Strengthening institutional accountability and regulatory capacity; and 3. Addressing the structural inequalities and systemic harms that individual remedies alone cannot resolve. She emphasised that public institutions cannot outsource their accountability for decisions simply because they have outsourced the technology, and proposed that high-impact AI systems affecting people’s rights, access to essential services and livelihoods should
6bbd7b6f9a6e.summary: Research ICT Africa researcher Tshepiso Hadebe participated in a provocation panel on Africa's governance priorities at the AI threshold, discussing rights, remedies, and institutional capacity.

6bbd7b6f9a6e.why: Highlights African institutional capacity gaps and governance priorities for AI, aligning with ILINA's focus on context-dependent risk assessment and public-interest safeguards.

83e6ee54bc2d.snippet: Is Kenya’s Digital Backbone AI-Ready? At Nairobi French Week 2026, I delivered the opening keynote and joined an industry roundtable examining Kenya’s digital infrastructure and its readiness for the age of AI. Kenya has made significant investments in fiber connectivity, data centers and renewable energy. However, AI readiness requires a realistic assessment of compute demand, energy availability, affordability, latency, infrastructure resilience and the workloads we intend to support. I emphasized the need for a national AI workload mapping study, developed as a shared public good, to inform infrastructure planning, investment decisions and opportunities for distributed AI infrastructure. Understanding actual and projected demand will help align investments in data, compute and talent with Kenya’s National AI Strategy. I appreciated the exchange with Ifeanyi Odoh of Schneider Electric, James Wekesa of WIOCC, Wilgon Berthold TSIBO of Infranum, Clément Martineau of IXAfrica, Aurélien Bayart of Nokia and representatives of Airtel Kenya. Thank you to the French Chamber of Commerce in Kenya, the Embassy of France and Team France partners for convening this important discussion. French Chamber of Commerce Kenya Domitille Guilloton Nokia WIOCC Team Finland Kenya
83e6ee54bc2d.summary: Ambassador Philip Thigo called for a national AI workload mapping study as a shared public good to inform infrastructure planning and investment decisions aligned with Kenya's National AI Strategy.

845b6ef1cf32.snippet: AfrIGF 2026 | Highlights from Day 3 What makes digital public infrastructure truly public? And what would an African-defined AI safety agenda look like? The discussion challenged assumptions about how DPI is defined and what it means for digital infrastructure to be genuinely public in African contexts. Participants then turned to the technical and regulatory challenges of digital identity systems, examining how their design and governance can enable inclusion or reinforce exclusion. 🤖 Beyond Imported Checklists: Toward an African AI Safety Agenda Drawing on RIA's Just AI Framework of Inquiry and the proceedings of our Just AI conference, this session questioned whether prevailing global AI safety frameworks adequately account for the risks and harms experienced across Africa. 845b6ef1cf32.summary: Day 3 of the African Internet Governance Forum featured a workshop on Digital Public Infrastructure defining what makes DPI truly public in African contexts, and a session on building an African-defined AI safety agenda grounded in local realities.

85ffecb39780.snippet: Language Undefined FAQ Livestream · Coming soon Date: Monday, 23 November 2026 Time: 9:00–17:00 AST (UTC−4) Location: Wyndham Grand Barbados, Sam Lord’s Castle About the Summit On 23 November 2026, the Government of Barbados and the United Nations will co-host the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Bridgetown, Barbados. The Summit will be attended by Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley of Barbados and UN Secretary-General António Guterres. The Summit comes at a critical moment for international cooperation on AI: while the risks and opportunities of AI cross borders, many countries have limited capacity to assess or influence the systems affecting them. The Summit will look at where international cooperation can improve AI safety and preparedness, and how countries and communities can shape AI development and benefit from it. The agenda covers risk management, inclusion, access, capacity, diffusion, and cultural and linguistic representation. Participants are expected to include senior representatives from governments, technology companies, the scientific community, civil society, international organizations and United Nations system entities. Co-hosts of the Summit H.E. Mia Amor Mottley Prime Minister of Barbados António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations Opening fireside chat moderator Nicholas Thompson CEO of The Atlantic Agenda Tentative programme. 876597cfb3e1.snippet: Nairobi, Kenya, you absolutely made last week count. Over the past week, we brought together policymakers, regulators, developers, mentors, judges, researchers, industry leaders, and ecosystem partners to ask how Africa can help shape the development, deployment, and governance of agentic AI. From the African Agentic AI Design Challenge and the Policymakers' Workshop to our Global South discussions, technical consultations, and the #MCPDevSummit Nairobi, your insights made every conversation substantive and forward-looking. 885be74d9f30.snippet: This week the Global Center on AI Governance hosted two back-to-back workshops in Johannesburg, designed to bring stakeholder voices into South Africa’s forthcoming national AI policy. ➡️Workshop 1: AI Beyond the Formal Economy This session brought together civil society organisations and groups representing workers in the informal economy for a discussion on the effects of AI in the South African informal sector. We presented a baseline map of the current environment with particular focus on the informal economy. The map sets out the actors involved, the underlying conditions they grapple with and the wider governance landscape they operate under. Participants responded to it by identifying gaps, issues that need to be addressed, and how the map should develop further. The session included presentations from Masana Mulaudzi from the Global Fund for a New Economy, Dr Roland Banya (Ph.D) from Research ICT Africa and Phathutshedzo Manenzhe from The Competition Commission South Africa. The discussion will inform a charter on AI and South Africa’s economic future, which will set out shared priorities for economically just labour relations in the age of AI. ➡️Workshop 2: Aligning South Africa’s AI Future This follow-up consultation built on the first Aligning South Africa’s AI Future workshop we convened with Google on 3 September. From AI tools that analyse chest X-rays and prioritise patients for treatment, to chatbots offering health advice, artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping healthcare and research. But what happens when these technologies raise questions about privacy, consent, fairness and accountability? Join us for next week's IDM Seminar, featuring Dr Brandon Ferlito and Lexie Timina from UCT's EthicsLab. Drawing on practical examples, they will explore the ethical, social and governance challenges of AI in healthcare and research, with particular attention to African contexts. The discussion will offer an opportunity to consider how we recognise ethical concerns and navigate the responsible use of AI in practice. 📅 Wednesday, 25 November 2026 ⏰ 13:00–14:00 📍 Wolfson Pavilion Lecture Theatre, IDM Building, UCT 🎓 1 CPD point available for registered attendees. All are welcome. Join us for an important conversation about the future of AI in healthcare and research.

9336f7d90fdb.participation: Governments and stakeholders can engage with the Call; look for official UN channels or The Future Society pathways for formal submission processes
9336f7d90fdb.snippet: 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝟯𝟬 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 “𝗔 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀,” 𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱, 𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 United Nations 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿. In it, they call for companies to adopt transparent safety protocols - including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation; for governments to coordinate standards and strengthen transparency and capacity - including through shared AI incident reporting; and to explore creating an international institution able to set standards, verify compliance, and convene states when AI capabilities cross key thresholds. The political will is there. The question now is how to turn it into action. The Future Society recommends five actions governments can take to help achieve the objectives set out in the Call: ▶️ Agree on a minimum set of rules that prevent unacceptable risks ▶️ Establish which of these rules can already be verified via existing means ▶️ Fund and test the verification mechanisms that are still missing ▶️ Build the relationships that an eventual international deal will depend on ▶️ Raise the safety bar and expectations towards AI development. 🔗 Read the full piece here: https://lnkd.in/gapCAKQP #AIGovernance #AIPolicy #AISafety Nick Moës Toni Lorente Niki Iliadis Kathrin Gardhouse Anoush Rima Tatevossian Michelle Parker
9336f7d90fdb.summary: Over 30 country leaders signed a UN-led Call for Control of Frontier AI Models launched at the UN General Assembly in September, calling for transparent safety protocols, coordinated standards, shared incident reporting, and exploration of an international institution to set standards and verify compliance.

99b725ef693c.headline: African digital sovereignty and AI governance
99b725ef693c.participation: Open to diplomats, academics and policymakers who attended; public input not specified in the post.
99b725ef693c.snippet: How can African countries shape their digital futures when much of the technology they rely on is controlled elsewhere? The Nordic Africa Institute brought together African and Nordic diplomats, academics and policymakers to discuss how African countries can make better use of AI for economic and social development while reducing dependence on foreign technology providers. “Countries in Africa are trying to lead their youthful, multi-talented and tech savvy populations into a future transformed by new frontiers of technology,” says Angela M., Senior Researcher at the Nordic Africa Institute, who convened the discussion. “But there are persistent challenges, from a fragmented legislative and regulatory landscape to limited internet access. There are divides that need to be bridged.” Key points from the discussion included: 🔹 Speed is an illusion, maybe even a false choice. African countries should take the time to work together on AI development and usage. 🔹 Education plays a major role in creating an enabling environment for tech entrepreneurs. 🔹 African agency is possible: hundreds of African laws, regulations and policies introduced. 🔹 Digital sovereignty is not only about money and infrastructure, but also about political will and integrating technology with African languages, cultures, rights and needs. Thank you to the speakers Seydina M. Ndiaye, Jane Munga, James Muriithi and Gustavo de Carvalho, and to the diplomats and policymakers who took part. #ScienceToPolicy #Dig
99b725ef693c.summary: Nordic Africa Institute convened African and Nordic diplomats, academics and policymakers to discuss how African countries can use AI for development while reducing dependence on foreign technology providers.
99b725ef693c.title: How can African countries shape their digital futures when much of the technology they rely on is controlled elsewhere? The Nordic Africa In
99b725ef693c.why: Addresses African agency in AI development, digital sovereignty, and the need for integrated policies — core to ILINA's governance and sovereignty priorities.

a344acbf915a.snippet: Call for Expressions of Interest | AI Beyond the Formal Economy As AI reshapes the world of work, are the needs and rights of workers in the informal economy being left behind? Findings from the Global Index On Responsible AI show that governments are in skills development for the AI economy, labour protections are lagging behind. The gap is most concerning in Africa's informal economy, where many people earn their livelihoods, yet national policies rarely address the realities of informal workers or small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Tp explore these challenges and potential responses, the Global Center on AI Governance, with support from Luminate though the Tech Justice in Africa project, is convening 'AI Beyond the Formal Economy: A Co-Creation dialogue for a Charter on AI and South Africa's Economic Future'. The one-day workshop will bring together trade unions, workers’ rights organisations, civil society groups working on economic justice, researchers and other stakeholders to: ▪️ Examine how AI is affecting workers and livelihoods in the informal economy and SMEs ▪️ Explore collective approaches to addressing emerging challenges ▪️ Contribute to a charter of shared priorities for economically just labour relations in the age of AI, with the aim of informing South Africa’s forthcoming national AI policy Event details 📅 Wednesday, 11 November 2026 🕤 09:30–16:00 SAST 📍 University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg (in person) We welcome expressions of interest fro

What would it take to build a more coordinated international response? A new discussion paper from the AI Governance for Humanity Lab, prepared to support and as a basis for discussion at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety on 23 November, outlines possible building blocks of a multilateral AI risk management framework. The paper builds on existing international instruments and calls, emerging national and corporate risk management approaches, and ongoing ethical, technical and scientific discussion on AI safety. ba8e2cb5b0bc.snippet: At the launch of the Global State of Responsible AI Report 2026, Dr. Jake Okechukwu Effoduh, Assistant Professor at the Lincoln Alexander School of Law, Toronto Metropolitan University, set out three reasons why public concern about AI does not always become public demand for accountability: 🔹 Tech determinism: AI is often narrated as inevitable, leaving people with a sense that there is nothing they can do about it. 🔹 Misplaced responsibility: When responsibility for AI is assigned to private companies rather than states, people are less likely to ask the state to address their concerns. 🔹 Masked harms: People in the Global South are disproportionately affected by AI systems in ways they may never know, from university admissions abroad to visa applications and job applications. The report highlights similar issues. Only 18% of countries require governments to disclose the algorithmic systems they use. Without that disclosure, people cannot know when AI has shaped a decision about them, let alone challenge it. He also highlighted what sets the report apart. It “reads the scores and not just reports them”, going back to the evidence behind each score in the @Global Index on Responsible AI to ask why a country sits where it does and what happens after a policy is adopted. ▶️ Watch the event recording: https://lnkd.in/gvBixnGw 🔗 Download the report: https://lnkd.in/gBWzheVi

c0aa9f39f84e.snippet: Paris Call for AI Safety and Security | Advancing Global Cooperation 🇫🇷 Participated in the high-level meeting convened by President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace, advancing international cooperation on AI safety and security. The Paris Call builds on the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models, endorsed by H.E. President William Ruto, and advances cooperation on independent evaluations, common standards and incident preparedness. In my intervention, I reiterated President Ruto’s priorities from the AI Middle Powers dialogue at UNGA81, particularly technological agency, shared capabilities and meaningful participation of the Global South. I emphasised three priorities: 1. Independent AI evaluations: Building scientific and institutional capacity in the Global South, including evaluations that reflect African languages and local contexts, supported by cooperation through NAAIMES. 2. AI security and incident preparedness: Strengthening early warning, incident reporting, information-sharing and coordinated responses to emerging frontier AI risks. 3. Shared capabilities and standards: Expanding access to compute, talent and evaluation infrastructure, while ensuring developing countries participate meaningfully in shaping international AI standards. Appreciation to President Macron and the French Government for convening this important engagement and advancing practical international cooperation. 🔗 https://lnkd.in/ezUGwwUA Emmanuel Macron Alexander Stubb Mark Carney

ceaaf2dee423.participation: Read the review; no direct participation required
ceaaf2dee423.snippet: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. All redactions that were important to our conclusions are described in the report below. Executive summary We agree with Anthropic that catastrophic risks from July 15th models were low, but we think it is plausible that they had crossed their early warning threshold at the time. METR reviewed the “Risks from automated R&D” section of Anthropic’s public August 2026 Risk Report . 1 We conducted this review as part of a high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration, in which Anthropic shared a private version of the Risk Report along with extensive other non-public data. Alongside this review, we are publishing a holistic assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic . This was conducted by the same METR employees as this Risk Report Review. Overall, we agree with Anthropic that by July 15th, internally deployed models posed low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains or causing acute catastrophic risks from acceleration of capabilities progress. However, the report’s claim that they had not crossed their early warning thresholds relies on contestable judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly in the public report. While both METR’s researchers on this project
ceaaf2dee423.summary: METR reviews Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report section on automated R&D, finding that while Anthropic claims their early warning thresholds were not crossed, METR considers this judgment contestable and believes the public report understates the level of AI R&D acceleration occurring.
ceaaf2dee423.title: Review of the "Risks from automated R&D" section in Anthropic's Risk Report (August 2026)
ceaaf2dee423.why: This review of AI R&D acceleration capabilities and threshold assessments is directly relevant to ILINA's position on AI safety and AI security given fragile states, and contributes to understanding frontier AI risk evaluation methods.

d268634fa3e5.snippet: Voor een marktkramer in Nairobi is een AI-incident geen abstract risico Jane Munga schetst in Rest of World een scenario: 6 uur 's ochtends op de groothandelsmarkt van Nairobi, en M-Pesa valt uit. In Accra gebeurt tegelijk hetzelfde met MoMo. Mobiel geld is daar basisinfrastructuur. Van de ruim 2.000 miljard dollar die in 2025 wereldwijd via mobiel geld circuleerde, liep 1.400 miljard via Afrika ten zuiden van de Sahara. Wie leeft van wat hij die dag verkoopt, heeft zelden krediet of een sociaal vangnet. Eén dag zonder betalingen raakt ook de boeren en gezinnen verderop in de keten. Het risico is concreet. In juli braken OpenAI-agents tijdens een interne evaluatie in bij Hugging Face. In juni kregen ze toegang tot een Australisch overheidsportaal, wat pas in september publiek werd. Munga pleit voor menselijke override, segmentatie, auditeerbaarheid en offline alternatieven, vanaf het ontwerp ingebouwd. Zelfs bij Hugging Face stuurde het eigen detectiesysteem het alarm aanvankelijk niet door naar de wachtdienst. PS: Zulke verhalen ontleed ik elke week in 'Het masker van AI': https://lnkd.in/eWX-BPpu #AIveiligheid #AIagents #Afrika #cybersecurity #mobielgeld #AI
d268634fa3e5.summary: Jane Munga argues Africa needs sovereign control over AI systems powering mobile money, citing scenarios where AI agent failures in Nairobi and Accra markets could devastate livelihoods, and calls for human override, segmentation, and offline alternatives built into system design.

d6b1a7735048.participation: Open attendance; look for side events, submission calls, or nomination opportunities linked to the summit programme.
d6b1a7735048.snippet: AI risks don’t stop at borders. Neither can the response. Recent cyber incidents and major technology outages have shown how quickly disruptions can ripple across borders. Their causes vary, but they raise a wider question: as AI systems become more capable and autonomous, are we equipped to manage the risks? On 23 November, the Government of Barbados and the United Nations will co-host the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety, with the Honourable Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley SC, MP. and UN Secretary-General António Guterres. Bridgetown will bring a distinct mix of participants into one room: political leaders from different regions, heads of AI companies, AI Safety Institutes, independent safety experts, members of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and civil society. The people building AI, the people studying its risks and the people responsible for governing it will be in direct conversation. At stake is both how we can manage increasingly powerful AI systems, and who has the capacity and voice to shape their future. Learn more: https://lnkd.in/g9CAEdcz #AISafety #AIGovernance #DigitalCooperation
d6b1a7735048.source: LinkedIn · United Nations Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies

ed0d7a8b3e70.participation: Sign the statement at https://www.aisafetyconnect.org/statement2026; organizations can add their name and share with one colleague
ed0d7a8b3e70.snippet: 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻 𝗮 𝗴𝗮𝗽 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲. 99 signatories have now asked them to limit recursive self-improvement (RSI) until it can be done safely. 𝗔𝗱𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁. AISC launched its Civil Society Statement on RSI with CeSIA (Center for AI Security) and The Future Society on 24 September at "Governing at the Speed of AI," our high-level evening on crisis preparedness during UNGA 81. The speakers in this video explain why it matters now. Yoshua Bengio warned that people can always be bought, influenced, and persuaded, leaving a weak link in any defense that depends on them. John Hartman of Minderoo said the incidents already seen in testing environments should be viewed as an early warning and not the final destination. Gabriela Ramos called our proposal essential, because recursive self-improvement is something we cannot manage. Pasi Rajala reminded the room that the tech companies themselves say we don't really have that much time to act. And President Juan Manuel Santos, member of The Elders Foundation, reminds us that we must act now because risk is increasing at a dangerously high rate. Today, frontier AI companies set, measure, and judge their own limits. The AISC Civil Society Statement asks governments to agree on a common threshold that is verified by someone other than the companies. It also calls for an independent authority with enforcement power, clear liability, real access for auditors, and international mechanism

f2110c7b0d20.headline: Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance
organizers: World Internet Conference (WIC) Specialized Committee on AI
f2110c7b0d20.participation: Review the full report PDF; no immediate call for input, but future annual editions may open consultations.
f2110c7b0d20.snippet: Five priorities for governing frontier AI, backed by contributors from China, Europe, Africa, Latin America and beyond. They come from “Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance,” the first report in a new annual series from the World Internet Conference (WIC) Specialized Committee on AI. AI Safety Connect contributed to it: our co-founders Nicolas Miailhe and Cyrus Hodes joined experts from governments, industry, academia and international organizations. The report was co-led by Zeng Yi of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance (Beijing-AISI) and Sean O hEigeartaigh of the University of Cambridge. The five directions for coordinated action: 1️⃣ Comparable model safety evaluations 2️⃣ Verification of safety commitments 3️⃣ Coordinated incident reporting and joint response 4️⃣ Governance of AI agents and open-weight models 5️⃣ Capacity building, so more countries can use evaluation tools and methods Many of these are the same priorities our panelists raised at Governing at the Speed of AI, our event at the UN General Assembly in New York in September. When people working in very different systems arrive at the same list, the open question is no longer what matters. It’s how to turn these priorities into shared practice, and that takes sustained dialogue across borders. That’s the work AISC exists to support. 📄 Link to the full report in the first comment. 👇 #AISafety #AIGovernance
f2110c7b0d20.summary: First annual report from the World Internet Conference Specialized Committee on AI, outlining five priorities for governing frontier AI: comparable model safety evaluations, verification of safety commitments, coordinated incident reporting, governance of AI agents and open-weight models, and capacity building.

About the International AI Safety Report
The International AI Safety Report is the world's first comprehensive review of the latest science on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. The work was overseen by an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by over 30 countries and intergovernmental organisations. Written by over 100 independent experts and led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, it represents the largest international collaboration on AI safety research to date. The Report provides decision-makers in government and beyond with a shared and authorative global picture of AI's risks and impacts.
3 February 2026
Annual Report
International AI Safety Report 2026
The second International AI Safety Report, published in February 2026, is the next iteration of the comprehensive review of latest scientific research on the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI systems. Led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio and authored by over 100 AI experts, the report is backed by over 30 countries and international organisations. It represents the largest global collaboration on AI safety to date.
Translated versions in the other 5 official UN languages can be found under the 'More Languages' button. The 'Extended Summary for Policymakers' can be found on the main 'Publications' page.
3 February 2026
Summary
2026 Report: Extended Summary for Policymakers
The Extended Summary for Policymakers provides a detailed (20 page) summary of the full 2026 Report. It includes the Report’s key findings and figures, concrete examples and a list of notable developments since the 2025 edition. It is structured around three central questions: what can general-purpose AI do today, what emerging risks does it pose, and how can those risks be mitigated?
Translated versions in the other 5 official UN languages can be found under the 'More Languages' button.
3 February 2026
Summary
2026 Report: Executive Summary
The Executive Summary offers a concise three-page overview of the 2026 Report’s core findings on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks, and risk management approaches. It covers how AI capabilities are advancing, what real-world evidence is emerging for key risks, and progress and remaining limitations in technical, institutional, and societal risk management measures.
25 November 2025
Key update
Second Key Update: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management
This Key Update examines developments in technical approaches to general-purpose AI risk management, from training models to refuse harmful requests to watermarking AI-generated content. Since the publication of the 2025 International AI Safety Report, the number of companies publishing Frontier AI Safety Frameworks has more than doubled, and researchers have refined techniques for training safer models and detecting AI-generated content. However, significant gaps remain: sophisticated attackers can often bypass current defences, and the real-world effectiveness of many safeguards is uncertain.

Together, We’re Building a Safer Digital Future for Asia
A global AI future where sovereign networks meaningfully help steer the trajectory of frontier technology toward public accountability, competitive plurality, and human flourishing.
Our Mission and Vision
Mission
Frontier AI is being built and governed by a handful of dominant actors, while most nations negotiate with them alone. AISA works to change that before the terms are locked in, focusing on collaboration and leverage Asia’s middle powers already hold.
To empower institutions across Asia to fully exercise the leverage they each hold over how AI’s infrastructure, technology and governance take shape globally.
Vision
A global AI future where sovereign networks meaningfully help steer the trajectory of frontier technology toward public accountability, competitive plurality, and human flourishing.
Trusted By
Building Trust at the Heart of
Asia’s AI Future
AISA serves as an agile, entrepreneurial partner to multilateral platforms and national institutions to strengthen AI governance in Asia.
Who we are →
Turning Ideas into Action for a
Safer AI Future
AISA helps institutions in Asia turn the influence they already hold into a practical counterweight, before decisions made upstream become impossible to reverse.
What we do →
Curate
We help governments map national dependencies and connect them with frontier-risk scientists to ground policy in objective analysis.
Inform
We translate technical foresight into actionable, enforceable safeguards, ensuring governments can negotiate from a clear view of their country’s bargaining power.
Catalyse
We maintain invitation-only channels for senior officials and diplomats across key bridge states to achieve minimum viable alignment before formal international negotiations.
Knowledge that Drives Change
Evidence-based insights from AISA’s Curate, Inform, and Catalyse programmes across Asia.
Report
Stronger Together: ASEAN in the AI Hardware Supply Chain
Southeast Asia is a key part of the AI hardware supply chain. Prepared with Metaculus after the 49th ASEAN Summit, this outlook pairs trade data with forecasts to show where the region stands and how, by negotiating together, members can gain more say over the terms of their role.
Read more →
Report
Scaling AI Diplomacy - How to use scenario exercises to building capacity and readiness
This policy report draws on a tabletop exercise convened alongside the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, arguing that there is an urgent need for countries to invest in preparedness through simulating crisis scenarios.
Read it there →
Insight
The World Doesn't Need Another UN AI Declaration. It Needs Architecture.
Writing in Tech Policy Press, AISA argues the UN's Global Dialogue on AI Governance must move past symbolic declarations, and build capacity across the Global Majority, put affected communities at the centre of governance design, and form a route to addressing catastrophic risk.
Read it there →
Insight
AI Safety Governance, The Southeast Asian Way: Bridging Global North Leadership with Regional Realities
A landmark collaboration between AI Safety Asia and the Brookings Institution charts a new course for inclusive AI governance
Read more →
Report
AI Safety Governance, the Southeast Asian Way
A report on AI governance across eleven Southeast Asian countries, drawing on AISA’s regional roundtables. It argues that localised, culturally informed regulation coordinated through ASEAN offers lessons for other emerging economies balancing innovation with safety.

Questions and Answers about GIZ
What is GIZ?
The Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH is a federal enterprise with worldwide operations. It supports the German Federal Government and many other public and private clients in achieving their goals in international cooperation for sustainable development and international education work. Together with its partners, GIZ has been developing effective solutions that offer people better prospects and improve their living conditions for more than 50 years.
GIZ is wholly owned by the German Federal Government. As a shareholder, the Federal Government is represented by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and the German Ministry of Finance (BMF).
How does GIZ work?
We work in almost 120 countries worldwide. All projects are based on a specific mandate – for example from the German Federal Government, national and international clients or the private sector.
We offer a wide range of services: we advise policy-makers and the private sector locally in our partner countries, for example on economic development and employment promotion, energy and the environment and peace and security. Our work focuses on developing and strengthening the capacities of individuals, organisations and governments. We see this as the key to sustainable development – and sustainability is the principle that guides our actions and core business. A specific example is the work we do to support countries in driving digital transformation and implementing measures to counter disinformation. We develop strategies for fair skilled labour migration, manage construction and infrastructure projects and assist people in dealing with the impacts of climate change.
Who commissions GIZ?
Our work is financed by public and private funds. We use these funds in a targeted manner to achieve the best possible results. Our main commissioning party is the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ). In 2025, around EUR 3.2 billion of our business volume was commissioned by BMZ. A further approx. EUR 443 million was commissioned by other German public contracting authorities, such as the German Federal Ministry of the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMUKN) and the German Federal Foreign Office. We also support the federal states in implementing international development cooperation activities.
We also work for international clients such as the European Union, various UN organisations and foundations. National governments from all over the world, as well as the private sector, also commission us directly.
Who does GIZ work with?
We work with a host of partners around the globe. Stable partnerships bring together interests between Germany, Europe and our partner countries and are essential for our work. After all, change can be achieved only if we work together.
We cooperate with international and regional organisations and with stakeholders from civil society and the scientific and academic community. We work with local partners – often with the relevant national ministries, but also with municipalities and local organisations. In Germany, we maintain close contact with public institutions, foundations, associations and KfW Development Bank.
Furthermore, cooperation with the private sector is becoming more and more important. In partnership with us, companies can steer their activities so that their success also results in improved living conditions for people locally. We pave the way for more private involvement in our countries of assignment by advising them on the right framework conditions and making use of networks to bring potential partners together. Take hydrogen, for example: we provide advice on the market ramp-up of green hydrogen in countries such as Brazil, South Africa and Morocco. This supports local people and also opens doors for German businesses, helps the climate and makes an important contribution to Germany’s energy security.
What values guide GIZ?
We work to shape a future worth living around the world. In doing so, our actions are guided by the principle of sustainability. We firmly believe that social responsibility, ecological balance and economic capacity must go hand in hand if current and future generations are to live safe, secure and dignified lives. As a federal enterprise, we are also guided by the principles upheld in German society. We promote respect for human rights, equal opportunities and integrity. At the same time, we support the rule of law and the political participation of the population, and are also committed to fairness within our own company.
What relevance does GIZ's work have for Germany?
International cooperation is in the
interests of Germany
and Europe. It promotes peace, security and prosperity worldwide – including here at home. Our work is not only effective locally for every single person we support, but also in the almost 120 countries in which we operate, as it creates more stable conditions. Moreover, what we achieve in the rest of the world also has an impact here in Germany and Europe. For example, we help companies to open up new markets, secure jobs and attract skilled labour, we create prospects and reduce the root causes of displacement, and we ensure energy security and stable raw material supply chains. As an export nation, Germany is particularly dependent on stable partnerships and international cooperation to maintain its own prosperity. Our contribution to this is significant.
Is GIZ a public-benefit organisation?
GIZ is a corporation in the legal form of a limited liability company under German law (GmbH), which is recognised as having a public-benefit status due to its corporate purpose. It is not our aim to maximise financial profit. We think in an entrepreneurial way and act cost-effectively; however, we are not profit-driven. We focus on supporting public welfare as part of our corporate purpose.
We generate the majority of our revenue (almost EUR 4 billion in 2025) through the German federal government and other public-sector clients in Germany. These commissions are exempt from corporation and trade tax. Commissions from other clients, such as the European Commission, are taxed in accordance with German income tax regulations. However, even with these commissions, GIZ does not focus on making a profit. GIZ works on a cost-covering basis and also retains a small risk premium for these commissions to cover the entrepreneurial risk. Surplus profits are used for further international cooperation projects in line with the company’s purpose.
What is GIZ's business volume?
In 2025, GIZ’s business volume was almost EUR 4 billion. Around EUR 3.7 billion of this was commissioned by federal ministries and other public sector clients in Germany. Business worth EUR 295 million was commissioned and financed by international clients from industrialised, emerging and developing countries.
Who manages GIZ?
GIZ is managed by a three-person
Management Board
. Thorsten Schäfer-Gümbel is Chair of the Management Board. The other members are Ingrid-Gabriela Hoven and Anna Sophie Herken.
When was GIZ established?
GIZ was established on 1 January 2011 as the result of a merger between three organisations: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit (GTZ) GmbH, the German Development Service (DED) gGmbH and Internationale Weiterbildung und Entwicklung gGmbH (InWEnt; Capacity Building International, Germany).
Where is GIZ based?
GIZ has two registered offices in Germany: one in Bonn and one in Eschborn, near Frankfurt am Main.
How many employees does GIZ have?
As at 31 December 2025, a total of 23,787 people were working for GIZ in almost 120 countries – with 5,640 employed in Germany and 2,324 seconded abroad. 15,823 people worked as local staff in the partner countries. Overall, almost two thirds of GIZ employees work abroad. In 2025, GIZ’s workforce also included 184 development workers.
All relevant figures can be found in GIZ’s latest
company report

About Lawyers Hub
The Lawyers Hub is a Pan-African digital law and policy organisation working at the confluence of law and technology, founded in 2018 and headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya. We work across all 54 African jurisdictions to make tech regulations and digital policies relevant, inclusive and searchable.
We convene Africa’s largest law and tech forum, build capacity through the Africa Digital Policy Institute, an official training partner of the International Association of Privacy Professionals, and the Africa Startup Law Accelerator, measure the continent’s AI governance through the Africa AI Governance Index, and carry African positions into continental and multilateral processes, from the African Union Data Policy Framework to the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance.Through this work we have reached over 28,000 leaders in law and technology across 41 countries.

Africa Startup Law Accelerator
The Africa Startup Law Accelerator is the premier African legal-tech accelerator program run annually by the Lawyers Hub that supports early-stage and growth-stage legal-tech startups in Africa to scale.
Motivated by the missing link between legal-tech innovators and legal practitioners targeted to benefit from developed legal technologies, the access to legal support gap for startups seeking affordable legal services, and the access to justice gap for ordinary Africans seeking user-friendly justice services, the accelerator endeavors to bridge these gaps.

The Africa Law Tech Festival
The Africa Law Tech Festival is the largest Law and Tech conference in Africa, convening over 2000 delegates from 40+ countries. It is an annual conference designed to appeal to a wide array of players in the legal & tech space through a multifaceted approach to conferencing.
The festival brings together like-minded individuals to lead idea-focused conversations and further innovation around technology and the law. Since 2020, the festival has hosted several relevant digital policy themes keeping with the rapid growth of the tech policy landscape on the African continent.

Global Dialogue on AI Governance
3–4 May 2027 | New York
As artificial intelligence advances rapidly, international cooperation on its governance is more important than ever. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance brings governments and stakeholders from every region together for inclusive discussions informed by independent science.
Sign up for updates
Meet the 2027 Co-Chairs
On 16 October 2026, the President of the General Assembly appointed two Permanent Representatives as Co-Chairs of the 2027 Dialogue, in line with General Assembly resolution 79/325.
Read the appointment letter for the 2027 Co-Chairs
See consultations for the 2027 Dialogue
H.E. Ms. Mutryce Agatha Williams
Permanent Representative of Saint Kitts and Nevis to the United Nations
H.E. Mr. Jihoon Cha
Permanent Representative of the Republic of Korea to the United Nations
The inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva, 6–7 July 2026. UN Photo/Elma Okic
About the Dialogue
Established by General Assembly resolution 79/325, adopted by consensus on 26 August 2025, the Dialogue builds directly on the Global Digital Compact. It is the first global platform of its kind dedicated to AI governance and is open to all Member States.
Each year, it brings governments together with the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community to exchange best practices, foster common approaches and help ensure AI governance reflects the priorities of all countries.
The 2027 Dialogue will take place back-to-back with the
12th Multi-Stakeholder Forum on Science, Technology and Innovation for the Sustainable Development Goals
Independent science informing the Dialogue
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI provides evidence-based assessments of AI's opportunities, risks and impacts. The Panel's next annual report will inform the 2027 Dialogue.
Learn more about the Scientific Panel
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI presents its Preliminary Report at the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on 6 July 2026. UN Photo/Elma Okic
2026 Dialogue: Geneva
The inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance was held in Geneva on 6 and 7 July 2026. Delegations from 163 countries took part, alongside representatives of the private sector, civil society, academia and the technical community. The 2026 Dialogue was co-chaired by H.E. Ms. Egriselda López, Permanent Representative of El Salvador, and H.E. Mr. Rein Tammsaar, Permanent Representative of Estonia.

Established with Resolution A/RES/79/325 on 26 August 2025, the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI serves as the first global scientific body on Artificial Intelligence (AI), bringing together leading experts to assess how AI is transforming our lives.
In a world where AI is racing ahead, this Panel will provide what’s been missing – rigorous, independent scientific insight.
António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
Background
The Global Digital Compact (
A/RES/79/1
), adopted at the 2024 Summit of the Future, set out a shared vision for an open, safe, and inclusive digital future. Among its commitments was the creation of an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI to advance scientific understanding and ensure that international deliberations are informed by the best available evidence.
The United Nations General Assembly established the
Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence

Resources
Building standards together: emerging technology ethics
UNESCO’s normative recommendations guide the ethical use of technologies, helping ensure they respect human rights, promote fairness, and benefit everyone.
Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology
The 2025 UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology sets global principles to ensure neurotechnology is developed and used in ways that respect human rights, dignity, and societal well-being.
Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
In 2021, UNESCO adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, guiding its work and helping Member States develop ethically aligned AI policies and capacities.
Our impact
How UNESCO is shaping an ethical digital future.
Education
We convene leaders, experts, and innovators to address the impact of AI and technology in education, promoting human-centered, inclusive, and equitable approaches to the benefit of all learners.
Gender
New technologies risk widening gender gaps, especially when AI learns from biased data. UNESCO’s work on AI and gender guides policymakers and innovators to close these divides.
Culture
As AI transforms how culture is created, accessed, managed, and experienced, UNESCO works to ensure AI’s development and use protect and promote cultural diversity, creativity, and access for all.
Green Digital Transformation
We foster global collaboration to make AI more sustainable, inclusive, and resilient for everyone.
Digital transformation
We promote a human-centered digital transformation, wherein AI, data, and open solutions build capacity, foster inclusion, protect diversity, and drive sustainable, rights-based innovation.
Quantum computing
We are helping the world prepare for the quantum revolution, wherein quantum mechanics helps solve problems too complex for today’s computers, in areas like medicine, encryption, and materials science.
Neurotechnology
We are developing ethical frameworks to ensure these technologies fulfill their promise in health while upholding equity, mental privacy, freedom of thought, and protection of the most vulnerable.
Natural science
We leverage AI to advance innovative, science-based solutions for sustainable development – from managing water and biodiversity to reducing disaster risks and strengthening climate resilience.
Information integrity
Algorithms and generative AI are reshaping how people access and trust information, with major effects on journalism, expression, and rights. We foster media literacy and inform digital platform governance.
Key initiatives
G20 Technology Policy Assistance Facility
A G20-backed platform that helps policymakers and stakeholders research, design, and implement ethical, inclusive, and future-ready technology and AI policies.
Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory
The Observatory supports global stakeholders in promoting ethical and responsible AI through research, tools, and best practices.
Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM)
The RAM program helps governments identify and address gaps in their AI policies, strategies, and legislation, so that AI is deployed ethically and responsibly to the benefit of their their citizens.
Internet Universality Indicators
This tool helps countries assess their Internet landscape, guide evidence-based policies, and foster inclusive, future-ready digital governance.
UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
The UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance brings together Member States and stakeholders to engage in the meaningful global conversation on AI that the world needs.
Coordinated by UNESCO and the ITU as the joint UN Secretariat, the Dialogue—mandated by the General Assembly—aims to ensure that AI governance reflects the priorities of all nations, not just the most technologically advanced. International cooperation on AI governance is essential to ensure that AI development benefits all of us.
